scenes.heading: Collecting data and sampling
scenes.say: How can asking just eighty students tell you what a whole school of fifteen hundred thinks? It works, but only if you choose those eighty students the right way. Let's see how.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: One spoonful tells you about the whole pot — if it is stirred
scenes.science: A random sample tells you about the population
scenes.breaks: Soup can be stirred until it is all the same. People can't, so we choose samples carefully.
scenes.say: A cook tastes one spoonful to check a whole pot of soup, but only after stirring it. Skim the oily top and you get the wrong idea. A good sample is a spoonful from a well-stirred pot. People can't be stirred, though, so we pick samples carefully.

scenes.heading: Population, census, sample
points: Population: the whole group you care about
Sample: data from part of the group
Representative: same mix as the population
scenes.say: The population is the whole group you want to know about. A census asks every member. A sample asks only some of them, which is faster and cheaper. A good sample is representative, meaning it has the same mix of people as the population.

scenes.heading: A systematic sample
scenes.say: First, forty people on a numbered list. Then we pick a random start, three, and take every fifth person: three, eight, thirteen, and so on. That is a systematic sample. The step, called the sampling interval, is the population size divided by the sample size.
scenes.caption: 40 people on a list. Start at 3 and take every 5th person: 3, 8, 13, … That is a systematic sample. The sampling interval k = population ÷ sample size.

scenes.heading: A stratified sample
notes: Each group gets its fair share
scenes.say: Here are forty-eight students: twenty-four in Year seven, sixteen in Year eight and eight in Year nine. A stratified sample of six takes from each group in proportion: three from Year seven, two from Year eight and one from Year nine.

scenes.heading: Estimating from a sample
scenes.question: 28 of a random sample of 80 students say yes. The school has 1500 students. Estimate how many would say yes.
scenes.say: Twenty-eight out of a random sample of eighty say yes. That's twenty-eight divided by eighty, or zero point three five. Apply the same fraction to the school: zero point three five times fifteen hundred is about five hundred and twenty-five students.
scenes.caption: 28 ÷ 80 = 0.35. Then 0.35 × 1500 ≈ 525 students.

scenes.heading: Watch out for bias
points: Selection: only some people can be chosen
scenes.say: Watch out for bias. Selection bias is when only some kinds of people can be chosen, like surveying at a gym. Non-response bias happens when lots of people don't reply. Leading questions push people to one answer. And online polls attract people with strong opinions.

points: Systematic: every k-th, k = N ÷ n
Stratified: fair share from each group
Check for bias before trusting results
scenes.say: Quick recap. A census asks everyone; a sample asks some. Systematic samples take every k-th person. Stratified samples take a fair share from each group. Always check for bias, and estimate by applying the sample fraction to the population. Now try the practice questions!
